To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the manager's optimal compensation increases with his ability; (ii) the manager's compensation is decreasing in his risk aversion and increasing in his ability persistence; (iii) when the manager's ability persistence is sufficiently high and his risk aversion is sufficiently low, the manager's compensation may increase over time, on average; (iv) when the manager is risk neutral or when his ability persistence is sufficiently low, on the other hand, the manager's expected compensation decreases over time.

(i) when the manager's ability to generate cash-flows is his private information, the optimal contract may include a non-linear compensation schedule that is time-dependent and, (ii) the optimal contract may be designed in such a way as to induce the manager to exert more effort as his ability increases.

(i) the manager’s optimal compensation contract is characterized by an increasing sequence of “dynamic wedges” that, in general, may increase or decrease with time and (ii) the manager’s expected utility is maximized by a contract that induces the manager to work harder in the early years of his career, but to take it easier in later years.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the optimal design of managerial compensation schemes when the ability of a manager to generate cash flows is unknown to the principal.
the optimal design of dynamic contracts for an agent whose productivity is private information and changes stochastically over time.
the optimal design of managerial contracts that reward managers for the cash flows they generate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the presence of ability persistence, distortions increase with tenure when the manager is risk averse enough.
the optimal dynamic managerial compensation contract is a combination of a linear incentive scheme, a bonus scheme, and a penalty scheme.
, in general, we do not know whether distortions increase or decrease on average with the manager's tenure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, under a certain degree of risk aversion, the longer the tenure of the manager, the more the principal can afford to pay him for exerting effort
we have developed a new approach for dynamic mechanism design that allows us to tackle directly a class of dynamic principal-agent problems that has not yet been studied in the literature.

, in a dynamic managerial compensation context, the “first-order” approach is more suitable when the manager's private information is persistent and the manager is risk-averse, and the “full program” approach is more useful when the manager's ability is less persistent, and/or when the manager's degree of risk aversion is lower.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the optimal dynamics of managerial compensation may be more complex than previously thought.
the optimal contract is not a static one, but rather it is a dynamic one that evolves with the agent's ability.
the optimal dynamics of managerial compensation depend crucially on the degree of persistence in the manager's ability and on his level of risk aversion.
